title: NEET UG 2026: exam held 3 May, re-examination on 21 June, result still awaited
content: NEET (UG) 2026 was held on Sunday, 3 May 2026 as a pen-and-paper test from 2:00 PM to 5:00 PM, as stated in NTA's official NEET (UG) 2026 Information Bulletin. Unusually for this cycle, the NTA also conducted a re-examination on 21 June 2026; provisional answer keys for that re-examination and the answer-key challenge window were published on the NTA NEET portal, and a fee-refund process was opened for candidates connected with the 3 May exam. As of 13 July 2026, the NTA had just issued a notice on the display of scanned OMR answer sheets and recorded responses. That means the NEET (UG) 2026 result and All India Rank had NOT yet been declared. Two practical consequences follow. First, any 'NEET 2026 cutoff' or 'expected rank' figure you see circulating right now is a coaching-centre prediction, not an official number, and should not be used to make an admission decision. Second, MCC counselling cannot begin until NTA hands the result data to the DGHS/MCC, so no MBBS/BDS seat allotment for 2026-27 has happened yet. Watch neet.nta.nic.in for the result and mcc.nic.in for the counselling schedule and the UG Counselling Information Bulletin for 2026, which MCC publishes after the result. Until the official result is out, plan around the rules of counselling rather than around a predicted score.

title: Qualifying percentile for NEET UG by category (50th, 40th, 45th)
content: To be eligible for admission to undergraduate medical courses you must score at or above a minimum percentile in NEET, and that percentile depends on your category. Per the NTA NEET (UG) 2026 Information Bulletin: General (Unreserved) and General-EWS candidates need a minimum of the 50th percentile. Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe and Other Backward Class (OBC-NCL) candidates need the 40th percentile. Candidates with benchmark disabilities under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 need the 45th percentile if they are Unreserved or GEN-EWS, and the 40th percentile if they are SC/ST/OBC-NCL. The percentile is calculated relative to the highest marks secured in the All India common merit list that year, so it is a rank-based, not a fixed-marks, standard: the qualifying marks move every year with the difficulty of the paper and the size of the candidate pool. Two things students routinely confuse. First, percentile is not percentage: the 50th percentile does not mean 50% marks, it means you scored better than roughly half of the candidates. Second, qualifying is not the same as getting a seat. The qualifying percentile only makes you eligible to enter counselling; the actual admission cutoff for any given college is set by supply and demand in counselling and is usually far, far above the qualifying mark. The bulletin also allows the Central Government, in consultation with NMC/DCI, to lower the minimum percentile for a given year if too few candidates qualify.

title: The last actual NEET qualifying cutoff: official NEET UG 2025 marks by category
content: Because NEET 2026 results are not out yet, the most recent OFFICIAL qualifying cutoff is from NEET (UG) 2025, published by the NTA in its result press release dated 14 June 2025. The category-wise qualifying criteria and marks ranges were: UR/EWS, 50th percentile and above, marks range 686-144, with 11,01,151 candidates qualifying. OBC (40th to below 50th percentile), 143-113, with 88,692 qualifying. SC (40th to below 50th percentile), 143-113, with 31,995 qualifying. ST (40th to below 50th percentile), 143-113, with 13,940 qualifying. UR/EWS with PwD (45th to below 50th percentile), 143-127, 472 candidates. OBC with PwD (40th to below 45th percentile), 126-113, 216 candidates. SC with PwD, 126-113, 48 candidates. ST with PwD, 126-113, 17 candidates. In total 12,36,531 candidates qualified out of 22,09,318 who appeared. For comparison, the same NTA table shows the UR/EWS qualifying range was 720-162 in 2024 and 720-137 in 2023, and the OBC/SC/ST range was 161-127 in 2024 and 136-107 in 2023. Note how sharply the cutoff moves year to year: a 144 that qualified in 2025 would not have qualified in 2024. Use these as historical reference points only. Do not assume the 2026 cutoff will land on any of these numbers, and treat any 2026 figure quoted before the NTA declares the result as a guess.

title: NEET exam pattern and marking scheme
content: Per the NTA NEET (UG) 2026 Information Bulletin, the paper has 180 compulsory multiple-choice questions to be answered in 180 minutes (2:00 PM to 5:00 PM). The subject split is Physics 45 questions (180 marks), Chemistry 45 questions (180 marks), and Biology, meaning Botany and Zoology combined, 90 questions (360 marks). The total is 180 questions for 720 marks. Each question is an MCQ with four options and a single correct or best answer. Marking is +4 for a correct or most appropriate answer, -1 for any incorrect option marked, and 0 for an unanswered question. The negative marking is what makes NEET a test of discipline as much as knowledge: reckless guessing has a real, compounding cost. The bulletin also spells out how flawed questions are handled. If more than one option is found correct, +4 goes only to those who marked any one of the correct options. If all options are found correct, +4 goes to everyone who attempted the question. And if none of the options is correct, or a question is found wrong or is dropped, then all candidates who appeared are awarded +4 for that question, whether or not they attempted it. Biology carries half the total marks, which is why a strong Biology score is usually the single biggest lever on your rank.

title: NEET age limit: minimum 17 years, and there is no upper age limit
content: A candidate must have completed the age of 17 years on or before 31 December of the year in which they appear for the NEET-UG examination. This is stated in the NTA NEET (UG) 2026 Information Bulletin, which cites the Graduate Medical Education Regulations 2023 (Amendment) dated 16 June 2023. For NEET (UG) 2026, the bulletin sets the lower age limit as candidates born on or before 31 December 2009, and this same date applies to all categories: General (UR), General-EWS, SC, ST, OBC-NCL, and PwBD/PwD candidates alike. On the upper end, there is NO upper age limit for NEET. The bulletin records this on the authority of NMC's Under-Graduate Medical Education Board letter No. U-11022/2/2022-UGMEB dated 9 March 2022. This is an important correction to a widely believed myth: older aspirants, repeaters and career-changers are not barred from NEET by age. You will still hear people quote an upper limit of 25 years (or 30 for reserved categories). That restriction was litigated and is no longer applied. There is also no NMC-imposed cap on the number of attempts at NEET-UG, so a student may reattempt in a later year. What does still bind you is the eligibility on the qualifying examination (Class 12 with Physics, Chemistry, Biology/Biotechnology and English) and the minimum percentile in NEET itself.

title: Class 12 subject and marks eligibility for MBBS/BDS admission
content: Passing NEET is not the only eligibility test; your Class 12 marks matter separately. As recorded in the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin, quoting NTA's eligibility conditions, a candidate must have passed Physics, Chemistry, Biology/Biotechnology and English individually at the qualifying examination, and must have obtained a minimum of 50% marks taken together in Physics, Chemistry and Biology/Biotechnology. For candidates belonging to Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes or Other Backward Classes (non-creamy layer), that aggregate requirement is 40% instead of 50%. For candidates with benchmark disabilities (PwBD), as per NMC and DCI regulations, the minimum in PCB taken together is 40% instead of 50% for Unreserved and GEN-EWS candidates, and 40% for SC/ST/OBC-NCL candidates. Note the structure carefully: you must PASS each of the four subjects individually, and separately clear the aggregate threshold across the three science subjects. English must be passed but is not counted in the PCB aggregate. A candidate whose Class 12 result has not yet been declared may be provisionally allowed to sit the entrance test, but cannot be admitted to the course until the eligibility above is actually satisfied. This is the clause that catches students out at the reporting desk: an allotted seat is provisional, and the allotted college will cancel it at document verification if the Class 12 aggregate falls short. Also note that marks in Mathematics are not considered for admission.

title: All India Rank (AIR) vs category rank, and how ties are broken
content: The NTA prepares a single merit list of all successful candidates in order of All India Rank (AIR), based on marks obtained in NEET. Your AIR is your position among every candidate in the country, irrespective of category. Your category rank is your position among candidates of your own category only, and it is derived from the same marks. So a candidate can have, say, a modest AIR but a strong OBC or SC rank, and it is the category rank that determines competitiveness against seats reserved for that category. Counselling authorities allot seats against the relevant merit list: MCC uses AIR for the 15% All India Quota, while state authorities draw their own merit lists from the AIR according to the categories candidates declared under that State's category list. Importantly, the NTA notes that when candidates apply to their State, they declare their category as per the STATE category list, and the state counselling authority makes its merit list accordingly; NTA has no role in domicile. This is why a caste that is OBC in one state may not be OBC in the Central list, and vice versa. Ties are broken by a defined sequence, per the NEET (UG) 2026 Information Bulletin: higher marks/percentile in Biology (Botany and Zoology), then Chemistry, then Physics; then a lower proportion of incorrect to correct answers across all subjects; then the same ratio in Biology, then Chemistry, then Physics. If a tie still persists after all of these, it is resolved by a random process guided by an independent expert committee. Note that older tie-breakers such as candidate age are no longer used.

title: What the 15% All India Quota (AIQ) is and why it is domicile-free
content: The 15% All India Quota is the share of MBBS/BDS seats in state government medical and dental colleges that is surrendered by the states to a central pool, and allotted by the Medical Counselling Committee (MCC) of the DGHS, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, on the basis of All India Rank. Its defining feature is that it is DOMICILE-FREE: you can compete for an AIQ seat in any participating state regardless of where you live or where you studied. The MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin lists the seats that make up the open, domicile-free pool: the 15% AIQ MBBS/BDS seats of the states, 100% of MBBS seats at all AIIMS across India, JIPMER (Puducherry and Karaikal), 100% MBBS/BDS seats of BHU (open), AMU (open), the Faculty of Dentistry at Jamia Millia Islamia (open), the 15% AIQ seats of Delhi University and IP University (VMMC, ABVIMS, ESIC Dental), and the 15% AIQ seats of ESIC. Alongside these, MCC also conducts counselling for 100% of Deemed University seats, Central Universities including their institutional/domicile quota, ESIC, AFMC Pune (registration part only), and B.Sc Nursing for central institutes. The eligibility conditions for AIQ are simply that you have qualified NEET-UG, that it is domicile-free, and that you meet NMC norms. There are four rounds of AIQ counselling: Round 1, Round 2, Round 3 and a Stray Vacancy Round. The remaining 85% of state college seats are handled separately by each state's own counselling authority.

title: Reservation in the 15% All India Quota
content: For the 15% All India Quota, MCC applies the Central Government's reservation policy, not the reservation policy of the state in which the college happens to sit. As set out in the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin, the AIQ reservation is: Scheduled Caste 15%, Scheduled Tribe 7.5%, Other Backward Classes (non-creamy layer, as per the CENTRAL OBC list) 27%, EWS as per Central Government norms 10%, and PwD 5% as horizontal reservation per NMC norms. The roster on the 15% AIQ seats is applied by MCC of DGHS as per DoPT, MoHFW and Government of India norms. Two consequences catch students out. First, the OBC benefit in AIQ requires your sub-caste to appear in the CENTRAL OBC list and requires a non-creamy-layer certificate in the prescribed central format. Many candidates hold an OBC certificate valid in their own state whose sub-caste is not on the central list; such a candidate cannot claim OBC reservation in AIQ, though they may still be OBC for their state quota. Second, PwD reservation is HORIZONTAL, meaning it cuts across the vertical categories rather than forming a separate block of seats: a PwD candidate is accommodated within their own category's quota. Deemed universities are a separate story: there is no OBC/SC/ST/PwD/EWS reservation there at all.

title: The 85% state quota and domicile: why the rules differ in every state
content: Everything that is not in the 15% All India Quota pool is, broadly, the state's own business. The MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin is explicit about this boundary: for state quota seats, and for private medical and dental colleges under state authority, candidates must approach the appropriate State Government / Admission Authority / Directorate of Medical Education, and MCC states plainly that it 'will not be able to guide candidates in this matter'. The NTA likewise says that state counselling authorities draw their own merit lists from the All India Rank, applying the category the candidate declared under that state's category list, and that NTA 'has no role' in domicile. The practical meaning: there is no single, national domicile rule. Each state sets its own eligibility for its 85% quota, and the tests differ widely: some states key on where you did Class 10 and Class 12, some on a domicile or nativity certificate, some on a number of years of study in the state, some on the parents' domicile or state government employment, and some maintain multiple candidature types with different rules. Because these criteria change from year to year and are only authoritative in the state's own information brochure, you must read the current brochure of YOUR state's counselling authority before you register, and confirm which candidature type you qualify for. Do not rely on a coaching video or last year's rules. A student who registers under the wrong candidature type usually loses the seat at document verification, and, in MCC's rounds, can also forfeit the security deposit.

title: The MCC counselling round structure: Round 1, 2, 3 and Stray Vacancy
content: MCC conducts four rounds for AIQ, Central Institutes/Universities, AIIMS, JIPMER, Deemed Universities, AMU, BHU and B.Sc Nursing: Round 1, Round 2, Round 3 and a Final Stray Vacancy Round. The four-round structure follows the Supreme Court's order in SLP (C) No. 10487 of 2021 (Nihila P.P. v. MCC and Others). Each round follows the same shape: registration (with payment of the non-refundable registration fee and the refundable security deposit), choice filling and locking within the scheduled window, seat allotment processing, publication of the result on mcc.nic.in, and then PHYSICAL reporting with original documents at the allotted college. Registration carries forward in a useful way. If you registered and were NOT allotted any seat in Round 1, you do not need to register again for Round 2; the same applies from Round 2 to Round 3, and a candidate freshly registered in Round 3 who is not allotted a seat is eligible for the stray round. Fresh registration (with full payment of fees) is required for those who never registered in an earlier round, and also for candidates who resigned or did not report in Round 1 or Round 2 and want to fill fresh choices in Round 3. Fresh registration is done separately for the Final Stray Vacancy Round. Seat conversion (for example, unfilled reserved seats converting to open) is carried out during Round 3 for AIQ, Deemed, Central Universities/Institutes, AIIMS, JIPMER and B.Sc Nursing. Note that these are MCC's rounds; states run their own parallel rounds, often including a 'mop-up' round, on their own schedules.

title: Registration fee and refundable security deposit for MCC counselling
content: At MCC registration you pay two separate things: a NON-REFUNDABLE registration fee and a REFUNDABLE security deposit. The amounts depend on which pool you are registering for. These figures are from the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin for the 2025 cycle; MCC republishes the bulletin each year, so reconfirm on mcc.nic.in before you pay. For Deemed Universities: a non-refundable registration fee of Rs 5,000 (the same for all candidates) plus a refundable security deposit of Rs 2,00,000. So a candidate opting for Deemed pays Rs 2,05,000 at registration. For the 15% All India Quota, Central Universities (DU, AMU, BHU, Jamia Millia Islamia), AFMC, ESIC, all AIIMS, JIPMER and B.Sc Nursing: the non-refundable registration fee is Rs 1,000 for UR/EWS and Rs 500 for SC/ST/OBC/PwD candidates, and the refundable security deposit is Rs 10,000 for UR/EWS and Rs 5,000 for SC/ST/OBC/PwD. So a UR candidate pays Rs 11,000 in total, and an SC/ST/OBC/PwD candidate pays Rs 5,500. If you want to apply for BOTH government (AIQ/central) seats and Deemed University seats, you do NOT pay twice: policy requires you to pay only the HIGHER fee, which means you pay the Deemed amount of Rs 5,000 plus Rs 2,00,000. The security deposit is a behavioural bond, not a fee: it is refunded in full if you play by the rules, and forfeited if you block a seat and walk away.

title: When the security deposit is forfeited (and how to avoid losing it)
content: The refundable security deposit exists to stop candidates from blocking seats they never intend to take. The MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin sets out exactly when it is forfeited. The core rule: the security deposit is forfeited if a candidate who has been allotted a seat in the SECOND round or any subsequent round does not join that institution. It is also forfeited if the admission is later cancelled for any reason, for example where the candidate gave wrong information at registration on the basis of which a seat was allotted and then cancelled by the admission authority at reporting, or where the candidate fails to produce the required documents within the stipulated time. Round by round: a candidate allotted a seat in Round 2 who does not join gets the deposit forfeited. A candidate allotted a seat in Round 3 who does not report exits with forfeiture of the security deposit AND is eliminated from further rounds of counselling. In the Stray Vacancy Round, a candidate allotted a seat must join; if they do not, the deposit is forfeited and they are not eligible for further rounds. Note the asymmetry that students miss: Round 1 is the forgiving round. If you are allotted a seat in Round 1 and simply do not report, you can still move on without the deposit being forfeited under this rule. From Round 2 onwards, an allotment you walk away from costs you money, and from Round 3 it also costs you the rest of your counselling. Choose your Round 2 and Round 3 choices as though they are binding, because in effect they are.

title: How and when the security deposit is refunded
content: The security deposit is refunded only AFTER all rounds of counselling are complete, not after your own round ends. Per the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin: MCC notifies completion of counselling on mcc.nic.in and publishes the list of candidates eligible for refund. The Financial Custodian (the entity that collects fees on MCC's behalf) then initiates the refund within 15 days of that notification and completes it within 30 days. Once the refund is made, MCC publishes the refund details, including refund date and transaction number, on its portal. Depending on your bank, the money then lands in your account roughly 2 to 15 days after the Financial Custodian releases it. You do NOT need to apply for the refund; do not approach the Financial Custodian asking for it. Two hard rules cause most refund failures. First, the refund goes back ONLY to the exact card or bank account from which the deposit was paid. If you paid from card number ending 5678, the refund goes to that card and nowhere else. MCC will not entertain requests to redirect a refund to a different account. Second, you must keep that card or bank account ACTIVE until the refund completes; if it is closed, the refund fails, recovery is slow and legally cumbersome, and neither MCC nor the Financial Custodian accepts responsibility for the delay. So: never pay from a friend's, relative's or agent's account. MCC also confirms it pays NO interest on the security deposit, and that, per RBI rules, it cannot refund a security deposit to an NRI account.

title: What 'exit with forfeiture' means, and when you can no longer resign a seat
content: 'Exit with forfeiture' is MCC's term for walking away from an allotted seat and paying for it with your security deposit. Per the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin, it means that if a candidate is allotted a seat in the second round or a subsequent round of counselling and does not want to join it, they can still exit, but they lose the security amount deposited. The critical companion rule is the point of no return: once a candidate has JOINED the allotted seat after Round 3, they are no longer eligible to resign or surrender that joined seat. The bulletin states this directly, and the Round 3 rules repeat it: if you are upgraded in Round 3 you must take relieving from the Round 2 seat and join the Round 3 seat, and once joined, you cannot upgrade or resign from that seat. So the decision tree is: in Round 1, you may decline an allotted seat without forfeiture. In Round 2, declining costs you the deposit. In Round 3, declining costs you the deposit and eliminates you from further rounds. And after joining in Round 3, you are locked in for the year. Students who plan to 'take a seat now and drop out later if a better college comes' need to understand that this option is closed after Round 3 joining. If your genuine intention is to reattempt NEET next year rather than study at the allotted college, it is usually cleaner not to join at all than to join and then try to surrender.

title: Upgradation between rounds: how to keep a seat while trying for a better one
content: Upgradation is how you hold a seat in hand while still competing for something better in the next round, and MCC's UG Counselling Information Bulletin sets out the mechanics. If you are allotted a seat in Round 1 and want to try to upgrade in Round 2, you must opt for 'willingness to upgrade' AND you must physically report with original documents at the allotted college. That physical reporting is not optional: the willingness to upgrade is exercised against a seat you have actually taken up. The same pattern applies from Round 2 to Round 3. If you are upgraded in Round 2, you must take relieving from your Round 1 seat and join the Round 2 seat. If you are upgraded in Round 3, you must take relieving from the Round 2 seat and join the Round 3 seat, and once joined you can neither upgrade further nor resign. Crucially, upgradation is one-way and burns the old seat: candidates who get upgraded in Round 2 shall have NO claim on the Round 1 seat, and candidates upgraded in Round 3 shall have no claim on the Round 2 seat. You cannot change your mind and go back. In Round 2 and Round 3 candidates exercise FRESH choices, so treat each round's choice list as a new, considered decision rather than a copy of the last one. And remember the cost of drifting: a Round 2 or Round 3 allotment you then fail to join means forfeiture of the security deposit.

title: The Final Stray Vacancy Round: last chance, and strictly binding
content: The Final Stray Vacancy Round is the last round MCC conducts, filling seats still vacant after Round 3 plus remaining Deemed University seats. Per the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin, fresh registration is required for the stray round; carrying forward an earlier registration does not enrol you. Before the round, MCC shares data with the Centre and the States, and if a candidate's name appears in the list of allotted candidates in either central or state counselling, that candidate is ELIMINATED from the All India Stray Vacancy Round. In other words, you cannot sit on a state seat and simultaneously gamble on a stray AIQ seat. For Deemed Universities, MCC conducts the stray round as directed by the Supreme Court, per the order dated 12.12.2022 in I.A. No. 132614/2022 in W.P.(C) No. 267/2017 (Dar-us-Slam Educational Trust and Others v. Medical Council of India and Others). The binding rule is unforgiving: if a candidate is allotted a seat in the stray round, they HAVE to join the allotted seat/college. If they do not join, the security deposit is forfeited and the candidate is not eligible to participate in any further rounds. Treat stray-round choice filling with real care. Because it is the last round and seats are scarce, students often fill choices indiscriminately just to get something, and then discover they have been allotted an expensive Deemed seat they cannot afford, in a city they never intended, with no way out except forfeiture. Only list colleges you would genuinely attend.

title: Deemed universities: no reservation, no domicile, and a Rs 2 lakh deposit
content: Deemed-to-be universities are private institutions whose MBBS/BDS seats are counselled 100% by MCC, not by the states. Two features define them. First, per the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin, there is NO reservation for OBC, SC, ST, PwD or EWS candidates in Deemed Universities. Whatever category you belong to, in a Deemed university you compete on open merit. (Some Deemed universities do have Jain Minority or Muslim Minority quotas; MCC advises candidates to verify their eligibility for such a category before applying under it.) Second, eligibility is simply that you qualified NEET-UG, and it is domicile-free, so any qualified candidate from any state may apply. The financial commitment is what students most often underestimate. Registration for Deemed requires a Rs 5,000 non-refundable fee plus a Rs 2,00,000 REFUNDABLE security deposit, payable up front at registration. And the tuition itself is typically a large multiple of a government college's fee. MCC explicitly warns candidates to confirm the fee structure and any additional fees from the colleges, especially Deemed Universities, BEFORE filling choices, and states that MCC takes no responsibility for college fee structures and will not entertain complaints about them. Choices once locked cannot be modified. The trap is well documented: a student fills Deemed choices as a 'backup' without checking the fees, is allotted one in a later round, cannot afford it, does not join, and forfeits Rs 2,00,000. Only fill a Deemed choice if you have actually checked that college's total cost and can pay it.

title: Private college fees: the NMC rule that 50% of seats are charged at government rates
content: By an Office Memorandum dated 3 February 2022 (No. NMC/US(NMC)/Fee-Regulating-Committee/2021-02), issued under Section 10(1)(i) of the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, the NMC laid down guidelines for determination of fees for 50% of the seats in private medical institutions and deemed-to-be universities. The core decision: the fee for 50% of the seats in private medical colleges and deemed universities should be AT PAR with the fee in the government medical colleges of that particular State or Union Territory. The benefit is first made available to candidates who have availed government quota seats, limited to 50% of the total sanctioned strength of that college or deemed university. If the government quota seats are fewer than 50% of total sanctioned seats, the remaining candidates get the benefit of a fee equivalent to government medical college fees, based purely on MERIT. The memorandum also lays down principles for fee fixation: no institution should charge a capitation fee in any form or manner; medical education must adhere strictly to the 'not-for-profit' principle, with no excessive expense or exorbitant profit component built into the fee; and fees should be based on the institution's operating cost, derived from its last audited accounts. In practice, implementation runs through each state's fee-fixation or fee-regulatory committee, and the extent of compliance varies. So do not assume the concessional rate automatically applies to you: check the specific college's approved fee structure with the state fee regulatory authority and the college itself before you commit.

title: MBBS fees can only be charged for 4.5 years, not 5 or 5.5 (NMC, April 2026)
content: In a Public Notice dated 7 April 2026 (No. CDN-13011/1/2026-Coordination-NMC), the National Medical Commission addressed a common billing abuse. It noted that certain medical colleges, institutions and universities were charging fees for the entire duration of five (5) or five and a half (5.5) years from MBBS students, and held that such practices are not consistent with the prescribed academic structure of the MBBS programme, because they charge fees for periods that do not constitute academic teaching. NMC pointed to Sections 10 and 24 of the NMC Act, 2019 read with the Competency Based Medical Education (CBME) Guidelines, 2024 framed under the Graduate Medical Education Regulations, which prescribe that MBBS comprises 4.5 years (54 months) of academic study followed by one year of compulsory rotating medical internship (CRMI). It also referred to the Supreme Court's interim directions in Abhishek Yadav v. Union of India (W.P. No. 730 of 2022), where grievances about non-payment of stipend and the imposition of internship-related charges were taken seriously, and to T.M.A. Pai Foundation, Islamic Academy of Education and P.A. Inamdar, under which fee structures must be reasonable, transparent, non-exploitative and commensurate with the facilities actually provided. NMC therefore DIRECTED that the fee for the MBBS course shall be charged only for the prescribed academic duration of 4.5 years, and warned that non-compliance would be viewed seriously. Practical takeaway: if a college's fee sheet bills you tuition for a fifth or an internship year, that is contrary to this direction; raise it with the college and, if needed, the state fee regulator and NMC.

title: NRI quota seats: who actually qualifies as an NRI candidate for 2026-27
content: MCC issued a Notice dated 27 May 2026 (Ref. U-11011/07/2025-MEC) specifically for candidates who claim to be NRI/OCI, or who want their nationality converted from Indian to NRI, for the NRI quota in UG/PG counselling for the academic year 2026-27. It sets out the eligibility criteria laid down by the Supreme Court in W.P. No. 13393 of 2007 and others (2008), Anshul Tomar v. State of M.P. Per the order as reproduced by MCC: if the mother or father of the student is an NRI ordinarily residing abroad, that is proper. If a first-degree relation of the student is an NRI ordinarily residing abroad, that too is considered eligible, and such a definition naturally includes the real brother and sister in addition to the mother and father. Where a person seeks to treat the student as their ward, that is acceptable subject to conditions: the person must be the NEAREST relation, drawn from a defined list of blood relations, namely the real brother and sister of the father (real uncle/aunt), the real brother and sister of the mother (maternal uncle/aunt), the father and mother of the father (grandparents), the father and mother of the mother (maternal grandparents), and first-degree paternal and maternal cousins. That person must themselves be an NRI, must ordinarily reside abroad, must have actually looked after the student as guardian with evidence produced to that effect, and there must be an affidavit to that fact. MCC has further informed candidates that for 2026 it will seek evidential proof and legal documents showing that the sponsor is genuinely the bona fide legal guardian of the candidate as per the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890. Distant-uncle 'sponsorship' arrangements sold by agents will not survive this scrutiny.

title: OCI cardholders: treated at par with Indian citizens for counselling
content: Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) cardholders had their eligibility thrown into doubt by a Government notification dated 4 March 2021, which was read as restricting OCI candidates to NRI/supernumerary seats. The Supreme Court settled the position in its judgment dated 3 February 2023 in W.P. (Civil) 891 of 2021, Anushka Rengunthwar and Others v. Union of India and Others, and MCC reproduces the operative part in its UG Counselling Information Bulletin. The Court declared that the impugned portion of the 2021 notification operates only PROSPECTIVELY, in respect of OCI cardholders who secured their OCI status after 4 March 2021, and held that the petitioners and all other similarly placed OCI cardholders remain entitled to the rights and privileges conferred on them before that notification. Following those directions, MCC states that OCI cardholders will now enjoy the rights they had prior to the 4 March 2021 notification: they are treated AT PAR with Indian citizens, and are eligible for UR (General) category seats as well as NRI seats in MCC's NEET-UG counselling. Note the boundaries. Being treated at par with Indian citizens for general seats does not hand an OCI candidate a reserved-category benefit: MCC's bulletin separately records that any candidate who is NRI, OCI, PIO or a Foreign National will NOT be shown seats reserved for other categories. Also, OCI/PIO/Foreign national candidates must produce citizenship certificate or card-number documents at reporting; these are mandatory.

title: Document checklist for reporting at the allotted college
content: The MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin lists the ORIGINAL documents (along with attested photocopies) required at the time of joining or reporting at the allotted medical/dental/nursing college. These are: the Allotment Letter issued by MCC; the NEET Admit Card issued by NTA; the NEET Result/Rank letter issued by NTA; a Date of Birth certificate (if the matriculation certificate does not carry the date of birth); the Class 10 certificate; the Class 10+2 certificate; the Class 10+2 marksheet; eight (8) passport-size photographs, the same as the one affixed on the application form; and proof of identity (Aadhaar, PAN, Driving Licence or Passport). For OCI/PIO/Foreign national candidates, citizenship certificate or card-number documents are mandatory. Category candidates must additionally carry, as applicable: an SC/ST certificate issued by the competent authority in the prescribed format, in English or Hindi, with the sub-caste clearly mentioned (if it is in a regional language, carry an attested English/Hindi translation); an OBC-NCL certificate as per the CENTRAL list, issued by the competent authority in the prescribed format, with the sub-caste tallying with the Central OBC list and the candidate not belonging to the creamy layer; and an EWS certificate in the prescribed format. MCC also advises checking the allotted college's own information for any additional document it may require. Two warnings from the bulletin. If there is a discrepancy in the spelling of your name across documents, carry an affidavit proving the documents belong to the same person. And if your originals are deposited with another institute, a letter saying so will NOT be accepted; you will not be allowed to take admission.

title: Physical reporting is mandatory and cannot be done by anyone else
content: An MCC seat allotment is not an admission. Per the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin, it is MANDATORY for candidates to physically report at the allotted college with their original documents in order to confirm the allotted seat, and no other person may submit the documents on the candidate's behalf. A parent, relative, agent or consultant cannot report for you. Reporting is also what makes an upgrade possible: a candidate allotted a seat in Round 1 who wants to be considered for upgrade in Round 2 must still physically report with original documents at the Round 1 college. Admission at reporting is provisional and subject to physical verification of your documents by the college authorities. MCC has no role in that verification, and states so expressly: candidates must have their original certificates with them at reporting. If your originals are lying with another institute, college or university, and you turn up with only a certificate stating that fact, you will not be allowed to take admission in the allotted medical or dental college. The deadlines are hard. MCC states that under no circumstances can the date of joining be extended by MCC. And the consequences of missing them bite: a Round 2 or Round 3 allotment you fail to join costs you the security deposit, and a Round 3 no-show also eliminates you from further rounds. Plan travel, money and documents well before the reporting window opens, not during it.

title: One registration only: multiple applications get you debarred
content: MCC's UG Counselling Information Bulletin opens with a set of conditions that are easy to skim and expensive to break. A candidate may submit the NEET-UG counselling application/registration form ONLY ONCE. Any candidate found to have submitted more than one application or registration form for NEET-UG counselling shall be DEBARRED from the NEET-UG counselling allotment process, their candidature shall be cancelled, and MCC of DGHS may take such further action as it deems appropriate. Applications can only be submitted online through mcc.nic.in; applications through any other mode will not be entertained. MCC further advises candidates to fill the form THEMSELVES on the MCC website, and not through an agent or third party. This advice is not decorative. The information you enter is treated as correct and self-certified, and MCC states that it will NOT, under any circumstances, entertain a request to change information provided by the candidate, and does not change, edit, modify or alter any information such as name, date of birth, category, nationality or contact details after submission. The data you entered at NTA registration is pre-populated into counselling and used as-is. Because the security deposit is forfeited where a seat is cancelled due to wrong information given at registration, a careless or agent-entered category, nationality or personal detail can cost you both the seat and the deposit. Finally, MCC reminds candidates that registering for counselling confers no automatic right to a seat, and that MCC does not allot any seat on a nomination basis or manually.

title: Choice filling and locking: the step most students get wrong
content: Choice filling is where counselling is actually won or lost, and MCC's rules around it are strict. Per the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin, candidates exercise choices and lock them during the scheduled choice filling/locking window. Once locked, choices CANNOT be modified, and MCC will not entertain any request to tinker with choices. MCC advises studying the seat matrix first and preparing a tentative, ordered list of colleges offline before attempting to fill choices online, and reading the candidate user manual before registering. Several practical points follow from the rules. Choices are considered in the order you rank them, so order them by genuine preference, not by predicted cutoff. Fresh choices are exercised in Round 2 and Round 3; your earlier list does not carry over, so each round is a fresh decision. Only fill a choice you would actually accept: from Round 2 onwards, being allotted a seat you then refuse forfeits your security deposit, and in the stray round it also ends your counselling. Before locking, confirm each college's fee structure, especially for Deemed universities, and check bond, stipend and course conditions, because MCC takes no responsibility for these and will not entertain complaints about them later. Also confirm your eligibility and domicile status before opting for institutional-quota seats of central universities, institutes or JIPMER. If you do not lock your choices within the window, you risk your choices not being considered at all. Do the research before the window opens; the window itself is for execution, not for deciding.

title: The most common and costly counselling mistakes
content: Almost every avoidable counselling disaster traces back to a rule printed in the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin. The most frequent: (1) Filling Deemed university choices as a casual 'backup' without checking the fees, then being allotted one, being unable to pay, not joining, and forfeiting the Rs 2,00,000 security deposit. MCC warns explicitly to confirm fee structures before filling choices. (2) Treating a Round 2 or Round 3 allotment as reversible. From Round 2 onwards, not joining an allotted seat forfeits the deposit; from Round 3, it also eliminates you from further rounds. (3) Submitting more than one registration form, which results in being debarred and candidature cancelled. (4) Letting an agent fill the form, then discovering a wrong category, nationality or personal detail that MCC will not edit, which can get the seat cancelled and the deposit forfeited. (5) Claiming OBC reservation in AIQ with a state OBC certificate whose sub-caste is not on the CENTRAL OBC list, or without a non-creamy-layer certificate in the prescribed format. (6) Turning up at reporting without ORIGINAL documents, or with a letter saying the originals are deposited elsewhere, which means admission will be refused. (7) Paying the security deposit from a friend's or relative's card, then finding the refund can only go back to that same account. (8) Skipping physical reporting after a Round 1 allotment while still expecting an upgrade, when reporting is required to stay in the upgrade path. (9) Assuming MCC can extend a joining date; it states it cannot, under any circumstances. Read the current year's bulletin cover to cover before you register. Every one of these mistakes is cheaper to avoid than to fix.

title: Bond, stipend and rural service obligations: verify with the college, they vary
content: Many government medical colleges attach a compulsory service bond to an MBBS seat: the graduate agrees to serve in a government or rural posting for a defined period, or else pay a penalty amount. Students constantly ask for a single national table of bond amounts and durations. There isn't one, and you should be suspicious of any site that presents one as fact. The MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin states the position plainly: information about stipend, fee structure, course duration, BOND AMOUNT, rendering of service in rural/tribal areas, NRI fees and other conditions is supplied by the medical colleges themselves, and MCC/DGHS takes NO responsibility for it, including for fees, bond, mode of payment or any typographical error in the data. It states that these conditions 'may vary from State to State and Institute to Institute', and advises candidates to visit the college website or contact the college authorities directly for any query on these points BEFORE filling choices. MCC collects college information and makes it available on its portal under 'College Information', and advises candidates to study that rather than relying on third-party websites. The practical rule for a student: before you lock a choice, get the bond terms in writing from the college or the state Directorate of Medical Education, including the years of service, the penalty amount, whether the bond is enforced in practice, and whether a PG seat pauses or triggers it. Bond penalties can run into lakhs, and since choices once locked cannot be modified and a refused allotment can cost your deposit, this is research to do BEFORE the choice window, not after allotment.

title: BDS as a fallback: what the course actually is
content: BDS (Bachelor of Dental Surgery) is the dental counterpart to MBBS, admitted through the same NEET-UG exam and the same counselling machinery, and it is the most common fallback for candidates whose rank will not reach an MBBS seat. Per the Dental Council of India's BDS Course Regulations, the undergraduate dental programme leading to the BDS degree is of 4 (four) academic years with 240 teaching days in each academic year, PLUS one year of paid rotating internship in a dental college. Every candidate is required, after passing the final BDS examination, to undergo that one-year paid rotating internship; the internship is compulsory, and the BDS degree is granted only after it is completed. So the realistic time to degree is five years, the same as MBBS. Eligibility mirrors MBBS closely: the candidate must have completed 17 years of age on or before 31 December of the year of admission; must have passed Physics, Chemistry and Biology with a minimum of 50% marks taken together at the qualifying examination (40% for SC/ST/OBC candidates); and must obtain the prescribed minimum in NEET. Marks obtained in Mathematics are not considered for admission to BDS. The NEET percentile requirement is the same structure as for MBBS: the 50th percentile generally, the 40th percentile for SC/ST/OBC, and the 45th percentile for candidates with locomotory disability. Admissions within each category are based solely on NEET marks, and reservation in dental colleges follows the laws prevailing in the respective State/UT. If BDS is genuinely on your list, fill it as a considered choice, not as a panic entry in a late round.

title: How many MBBS seats actually exist, and how many students compete for them
content: The arithmetic of NEET is the single most useful thing a student can internalise before making plans. On the supply side, the NMC's final MBBS Seat Matrix as on 03.12.2025 for the academic year 2025-26 (including AIIMS, INIs and JIPMER) lists 819 medical colleges with a combined 1,29,026 MBBS seats. Of these, 455 are government colleges offering 63,683 seats, and 364 are non-government colleges (trust, society, private and company managed) offering 65,343 seats. The same matrix shows the total rose from 1,17,750 seats in the previous year, so capacity is expanding quickly, but the government share is now slightly under half of all MBBS seats. On the demand side, the NTA's NEET (UG) 2025 result press release records 22,76,069 candidates registered, 22,09,318 appeared, and 12,36,531 qualified. Put those together and the picture is stark: roughly 12.4 lakh candidates qualified for about 1.29 lakh MBBS seats, that is, close to ten qualified candidates for every MBBS seat, and about twenty for every GOVERNMENT MBBS seat. This is why 'qualifying' NEET and 'getting an MBBS seat' are entirely different achievements, and why a student who clears the 50th percentile by a few marks should be planning realistically around BDS, AYUSH, B.Sc Nursing, allied health, or a considered reattempt, rather than assuming a government MBBS seat is within reach. Add BDS, AYUSH and nursing seats and the total pool widens, but the MBBS bottleneck is real.

title: AYUSH courses (BAMS, BHMS, BUMS, BSMS) and AACCC counselling
content: NEET-UG is the single entrance test for AYUSH undergraduate courses as well. Per the NTA NEET (UG) 2026 Information Bulletin, admission to ALL seats of the undergraduate Ayurveda (BAMS), Siddha (BSMS), Unani (BUMS) and Homoeopathy (BHMS) courses is done through NEET (UG), under the National Commission for Indian System of Medicine (NCISM) regulations of 2022 and the National Commission for Homoeopathy regulations. The qualifying percentile is the same structure as MBBS/BDS: a minimum of the 50th percentile, with the 40th percentile for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes, and, for candidates with benchmark disabilities under the RPwD Act 2016, the 45th percentile for the general category and the 40th percentile for SC/ST/OBC. Counselling for the 15% All India Quota in AYUSH is NOT conducted by MCC. It is conducted by the AYUSH Admissions Central Counselling Committee (AACCC), which operates under NCISM and runs online counselling for AIQ seats in government and government-aided colleges, along with deemed and central universities, covering BAMS, BHMS, BUMS, BSMS and B.Pharm (ITRA), as well as PG AYUSH courses. NTA's 2025 result press release confirms that AACCC is the counselling authority for AIQ for BAMS, BUMS and BSMS under NCISM, and also for BHMS under NCH. Two course-specific eligibility conditions are worth noting: for BUMS the candidate must have passed Class 10 with Urdu, Arabic or Persian as a subject (or clear a prescribed Urdu test), and for BSMS the candidate must have passed Tamil at Class 10/higher secondary, or study Tamil in the first professional year. State AYUSH quota seats are handled by the respective state authorities.

title: Studying MBBS abroad: the NMC rules that decide if your degree will count
content: If you are considering an MBBS abroad, the rules that matter are the NMC's Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate (FMGL) Regulations, 2021, which came into force on 18 November 2021. They apply to students who began their foreign medical education after that date; those who acquired a foreign degree, or were already pursuing one, before 18 November 2021 are governed by the previously applicable regulations. NMC's official FAQ on the FMGL Regulations sets out the conditions your foreign course must satisfy. The course leading to the foreign medical degree must be of a minimum duration of 54 months (four and a half years). The MEDIUM OF INSTRUCTION must be English. The course must cover theory, practical and clinical training equivalent to the Indian MBBS. You must then complete an internship of a minimum of 12 months IN THE SAME foreign institution where the primary medical qualification was obtained, with hands-on clinical training across the major clinical subjects. The entire course, training and internship must be done OUTSIDE India, in the same country that awards the degree: no part of the medical training or internship may be done in India or in a third country, and transfer to an Indian medical college for internship or exams is not permitted. The whole course must be completed within TEN YEARS from the date of joining. You must also be registered with the professional regulatory body of the country awarding the degree, on par with the licence given to that country's own citizens. Online classes are allowed for theory subjects only, supplemented by offline practical and clinical training, with a completion certificate required. A course that fails any one of these conditions can leave you with a degree you cannot use in India.

title: FMGE / NExT and the second internship: how foreign graduates get licensed in India
content: A foreign medical graduate (FMG), defined by NMC as a person who does not have their basic/primary medical qualification from any university, medical college or institution in India and who seeks a licence to practise medicine in India, cannot simply come home and practise. Per NMC's official FAQ on the Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate (FMGL) Regulations, 2021, FMGs have to clear the National Exit Test (NExT), or such other mandated test or tests conducted by NMC. The rule that surprises most families is the SECOND internship. NMC states that in addition to completing an internship of at least 12 months in the same foreign medical institution, FMGs are REQUIRED to undergo a supervised internship IN INDIA for a minimum term of twelve months. FMGs apply for this Indian internship with the respective State Medical Council through the National Medical Commission. To be eligible for that internship, the FMG must have: completed a course of at least 54 months; completed the 12-month internship in the same foreign institution; received the degree with English as the medium of instruction; studied the mandatory subjects in Schedule I; registered with the professional regulatory body of the country awarding the degree; passed the screening test / NExT; and obtained provisional registration from the State Medical Council. So the honest timeline for an MBBS abroad is: 4.5+ years of study, a year of internship there, a screening exam, and another year of internship in India.

title: Who conducts which counselling: MCC vs state vs AACCC
content: A great deal of student confusion comes from not knowing which authority owns which seat. The MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin draws the line clearly. MCC of DGHS conducts counselling for: the 15% All India Quota; 100% of Deemed University seats; Central Universities (Delhi University, AMU and BHU, including their institutional/domicile quota); ESIC; AFMC Pune (the registration part only); IP University seats (VMMC & Safdarjung, ABVIMS & RML, and ESIC Dental, Delhi, comprising 15% AIQ plus 85% institutional quota); 100% of AIIMS seats; 100% of JIPMER seats; and B.Sc Nursing for central institutes only. MCC states that its role is limited to allotting seats to participating candidates as per their merit and choice, and that this begins only after it receives the list of successful candidates from the NTA. For everything else, namely State Quota seats and private medical and dental colleges under state authority, candidates must contact the appropriate State Government / Admission Authority / Directorate of Medical Education, and MCC states it 'will not be able to guide candidates in this matter'. AYUSH courses (BAMS, BHMS, BUMS, BSMS) are counselled for the All India Quota by a third body altogether, the AYUSH Admissions Central Counselling Committee (AACCC) under NCISM/NCH. The practical implication: a serious candidate usually registers for MORE THAN ONE counselling in parallel, typically MCC for AIQ/Deemed and their home state's authority for the 85% state quota, each with its own portal, schedule, fees, documents and deadlines. Missing a state deadline because you were watching only the MCC calendar is a common and entirely avoidable way to lose a seat.

title: Seat conversion in Round 3 and why cutoffs move between rounds
content: Students often ask why the closing rank for the same college and category changes so much from Round 1 to Round 3, and whether it is worth waiting for a later round. Part of the answer is seat conversion. Per the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin, the conversion of seats is carried out during ROUND 3 for AIQ, Deemed, Central Universities/Institutes, AIIMS, JIPMER and B.Sc Nursing. Conversion is the process by which seats reserved for a category that remain unfilled are converted and offered to other candidates as per the applicable rules, which changes the effective supply in each category partway through counselling. The other driver is churn: candidates who are upgraded vacate their earlier seats, candidates who do not report release seats, and candidates who join a state seat drop out of the central pool. Both forces mean the closing rank in a later round can be markedly better or worse than in Round 1, and it is not reliably predictable in either direction. Two cautions follow. First, do not treat last year's Round 1 closing rank as a promise about this year's Round 3, or vice versa; compare like with like, the same round, the same quota and the same category. Second, waiting for a later round is not free. From Round 2 onwards, an allotment you refuse forfeits your security deposit; from Round 3, it also eliminates you from further rounds; and the stray round is binding, with elimination if you already hold a seat in central or state counselling. Strategy should be driven by what you would actually accept, not by hope that a late round will be soft.

title: PwD candidates: 5% horizontal reservation and the disability certificate
content: Candidates with disabilities have a specific route through NEET counselling and specific paperwork that must be right. On reservation, the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin states that PwD reservation in the 15% All India Quota is 5%, applied as HORIZONTAL reservation as per NMC norms. Horizontal means the PwD quota cuts across the vertical categories (UR, EWS, OBC, SC, ST) rather than existing as a separate block of seats, so a PwD candidate is accommodated within their own category's share. On eligibility thresholds, the NEET (UG) 2026 Information Bulletin sets a lower qualifying percentile for candidates with benchmark disabilities under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016: the 45th percentile for Unreserved and GEN-EWS candidates, and the 40th percentile for SC/ST/OBC-NCL candidates. The Class 12 requirement is also relaxed, with a minimum of 40% in Physics, Chemistry and Biology taken together instead of 50%. For scale, NTA's NEET (UG) 2025 result press release records 9,167 PwBD candidates registered, 8,842 appeared and 3,673 qualified. Two practical points. Disability must be certified through the prescribed process and, in MCC's cycles, through the designated disability certification centres within the notified window; MCC has run a PwD certificate portal with a hard closing date. And note there is NO reservation for PwD candidates in Deemed Universities. Get the certification done early; a late or non-conforming certificate is a common reason PwD claims fail at verification.

title: Percentile vs percentage vs marks vs rank: four different things
content: These four words get used interchangeably by students and they mean entirely different things, which leads to real errors of judgement. MARKS are your raw score out of 720, computed as +4 per correct answer and -1 per incorrect one, per the NEET (UG) 2026 Information Bulletin. PERCENTAGE would be your marks expressed out of 100, and NEET does not use it for qualification at all. PERCENTILE is your standing relative to the other candidates: the NEET bulletin specifies that the qualifying percentile is determined on the basis of the highest marks secured in the All India common merit list, so the 50th percentile broadly means you did better than about half the candidates. It is emphatically NOT 50% marks. This is why the 50th-percentile mark moves every year: NTA's official figures show the UR/EWS qualifying range was 720-137 in 2023, 720-162 in 2024, and 686-144 in 2025. The same 50th percentile corresponded to 137, then 162, then 144 marks. RANK (All India Rank) is your ordinal position in the merit list, and it is what counselling authorities actually allot seats against. The relationship between marks and rank also shifts each year with the difficulty of the paper and the number of candidates: a given score can map to very different ranks in different years, and near the dense middle of the distribution a couple of marks can move you thousands of ranks. Practical consequence: never compare your marks with a friend's rank from a different year, and never treat a predicted rank from a marks-to-rank calculator as anything more than an estimate until NTA publishes your actual All India Rank.

title: Qualifying NEET is not the same as getting a seat
content: This is the single most important misconception to clear, and the official numbers make it undeniable. The NTA declares a QUALIFYING cutoff, which is the minimum percentile that makes you ELIGIBLE to enter counselling. It does not declare an admission cutoff. In NEET (UG) 2025, per NTA's official result press release, 12,36,531 candidates qualified. The NMC's final MBBS seat matrix for the same academic year lists 1,29,026 MBBS seats across 819 colleges, of which only 63,683 are in government colleges. So roughly ten qualified candidates existed for every MBBS seat, and about twenty for every government MBBS seat. The ADMISSION cutoff, meaning the closing rank at which a particular college and category actually stops allotting seats, is set by supply and demand during counselling. It is published by the counselling authority after each round, varies enormously by college, category, quota and round, and sits far above the qualifying threshold for any desirable college. A candidate who scrapes past the 50th percentile has cleared the eligibility bar and is nowhere near a government MBBS seat. What that student should do is plan honestly across the full option set: BDS, the AYUSH courses through AACCC and state counselling, B.Sc Nursing, allied health sciences, or a considered reattempt at NEET, for which there is no upper age limit and no cap on attempts. Beware anyone, especially an agent, who tells you that a qualifying score can be converted into an MBBS seat 'through management quota' at a government college. It cannot; MCC states that it does not allot any seat on a nomination basis or manually.

title: Registration happens only on mcc.nic.in, and only after the NEET result
content: MCC's UG Counselling Information Bulletin is explicit about the channel and the sequence. Candidates seeking admission to MBBS/BDS on the basis of their All India Rank in NEET (UG) must register on the MCC website, www.mcc.nic.in, AFTER the declaration of the NEET (UG) result. The application for NEET-UG counselling can only be submitted online through mcc.nic.in, and an application submitted through any other mode 'shall not be entertained'. MCC's role begins only once the NTA hands over the list and data of successful candidates; MCC has no part in conducting the exam or in declaring the result. Candidates are advised to fill the form themselves, and NOT through an agent or third party. This sequencing matters right now: because the NEET (UG) 2026 result had not been declared as of mid-July 2026, MCC counselling for 2026-27 had not opened, and any website, agent or 'consultant' offering to register you for MCC counselling, or promising a seat, before the result is out is not doing something MCC recognises. MCC also cautions that registering for counselling confers no automatic right to a seat, that selection is subject to merit and eligibility criteria, and that MCC does not allot any seat on a nomination basis or manually. Candidates are deemed to have read, agreed to and accepted the scheme of counselling and its terms and conditions once they complete the online registration, so read the current year's bulletin before you click submit. Watch mcc.nic.in for the schedule and the year's Information Bulletin, which MCC publishes after the NEET result.

title: Central institutes: AIIMS, JIPMER, AFMC, ESIC, BHU, AMU and Jamia
content: Several of the most sought-after MBBS seats in India are not state seats at all, and they are counselled centrally by MCC. Per the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin, the open, domicile-free pool includes 100% of MBBS seats at all AIIMS across India, JIPMER (Puducherry and Karaikal), 100% of BHU's MBBS/BDS open seats, AMU open seats, and the open seats of the Faculty of Dentistry at Jamia Millia Islamia. MCC also conducts counselling for Central Universities including Delhi University, AMU and BHU (covering their institutional/domicile quota), for ESIC, for IP University seats (VMMC & Safdarjung, ABVIMS & RML, and ESIC Dental Delhi, which comprise 15% AIQ plus 85% institutional quota), and for AFMC Pune, though for AFMC only the REGISTRATION part is handled through MCC. Reservation at AIIMS follows the Central Government's policy, the same structure as AIQ: SC 15%, ST 7.5%, OBC-NCL (Central list) 27%, and EWS 10%. Because these institutes are domicile-free and admit on All India Rank, they draw the strongest candidates in the country, and their closing ranks are correspondingly severe. Two cautions from the bulletin. Candidates are advised to CONFIRM their eligibility and domicile status before registering for the institutional-quota seats of central universities/institutes and JIPMER, since those institutional quotas carry their own conditions. And AFMC has its own additional selection process beyond the MCC registration step, so check AFMC's own requirements directly rather than assuming MCC registration is the whole procedure.

title: What an MCC allotment letter does and does not guarantee
content: An allotment result on mcc.nic.in feels like the finish line. It is not. Per the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin, an allotted seat is confirmed only when the candidate PHYSICALLY reports at the allotted college with original documents, and admission is provisional, subject to physical verification of those documents by the college authorities. MCC has no role in that verification. The college can and will refuse admission if the documents do not support what you declared at registration: the bulletin notes that the security deposit is forfeited where admission is cancelled because the candidate gave wrong information at registration on the basis of which the seat was allotted, or where the candidate fails to produce the required documents within the stipulated time. Equally, registering and being allotted a seat confers no automatic right: MCC states that registering for NEET-UG counselling does not confer any automatic right to secure an undergraduate seat, and that selection and admission remain subject to merit, admission criteria, eligibility and the criteria prescribed by the respective university, medical institution, the Commission and the State/Central Government. MCC also states it does not allot any seat on a nomination basis or manually, and, once allotment is made through the online process, that allotment is 'firm and final' as per the Supreme Court's guidelines. So treat the allotment letter as an instruction to act, quickly and with correct paperwork, rather than as a guarantee. Verify the college's fee, bond and course conditions, assemble your originals, and report within the window, because MCC states that the date of joining cannot be extended under any circumstances.

title: B.Sc Nursing through NEET and the wider option set beyond MBBS
content: NEET-UG opens more doors than MBBS and BDS, and a candidate whose rank will not reach a medical seat should understand the full option set before defaulting to a reattempt. MCC conducts B.Sc Nursing counselling for CENTRAL INSTITUTES only, alongside its MBBS/BDS rounds; the registration fee and security deposit for B.Sc Nursing sit in the same bracket as the 15% AIQ and central university seats (Rs 1,000 + Rs 10,000 for UR/EWS, Rs 500 + Rs 5,000 for SC/ST/OBC/PwD), per the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin. The NTA's NEET (UG) 2025 result press release confirms that NEET result data is also utilised for B.Sc (H) Nursing courses in accordance with the relevant eligibility criteria and regulations, and that NEET data is used for admission to BVSc & AH (veterinary) courses under the 15% quota of the Veterinary Council of India in recognised veterinary colleges. AYUSH courses (BAMS, BSMS, BUMS, BHMS) are admitted entirely through NEET, with All India Quota counselling run by AACCC and state quota by the states. B.Sc Nursing seats outside the central institutes are handled by state authorities and other bodies, so check your state's portal. Given that roughly 12.4 lakh candidates qualified in 2025 against about 1.29 lakh MBBS seats, most qualified candidates will not get an MBBS seat, and a plan that includes BDS, AYUSH, nursing, veterinary or allied health is not a failure plan, it is a realistic one. Decide before the choice-filling window, because once choices are locked they cannot be modified.

title: Open School, private candidates and Biology as an additional subject
content: A long-running eligibility dispute affects a specific group of candidates, and the current position is set out in the NTA NEET (UG) Information Bulletin. The regulations as drafted provided that candidates who passed Class 12 from an Open School or as private candidates 'shall not be eligible' to appear for NEET, and further that a study of Biology/Biotechnology as an ADDITIONAL subject at Class 12 level would not be permissible. However, NTA records that this proviso was challenged and that the provisions disqualifying recognised Open School Board candidates, and candidates who studied Biology/Biotechnology as an additional subject, have been STRUCK DOWN by the High Courts (the Delhi High Court, the Allahabad High Court's Lucknow Bench, and the Madhya Pradesh High Court at Jabalpur). The National Medical Commission (erstwhile Medical Council of India) has preferred Special Leave Petitions before the Supreme Court and appeals before the High Courts. The consequence for candidates, in NTA's own words: the candidatures of candidates who have passed the qualifying examination, that is Class 12, from the National Institute of Open Schooling or State Open Schools, or as private candidates from recognised State Boards, or with Biology/Biotechnology as an additional subject, SHALL BE ALLOWED, but subject to the outcome of the Special Leave Petitions and appeals filed by the NMC. So such candidates may currently appear and participate, but their candidature is conditional on pending litigation and could be affected by the final judicial outcome. If you fall in this group, keep your documentation in order, follow the current year's bulletin closely, and understand that the position is not yet finally settled.

title: How to read closing ranks without fooling yourself
content: Closing ranks (the last rank allotted a seat in a given college, category, quota and round) are the main evidence students use to plan choices, and they are routinely misread. Four rules keep you honest. First, compare LIKE WITH LIKE. A closing rank is meaningless unless you know its round (Round 1, 2, 3 or stray), its quota (15% AIQ vs 85% state vs deemed vs institutional), its category, and the year. An AIQ Round 1 closing rank and a state-quota mop-up closing rank for the same college are different universes. Second, expect movement within a year. Per the MCC UG Counselling Information Bulletin, seat conversion is carried out in ROUND 3 for AIQ, Deemed, central universities/institutes, AIIMS, JIPMER and B.Sc Nursing, and candidates upgrading or failing to report keep releasing seats, so closing ranks shift between rounds in ways that are not reliably predictable. Third, expect movement between years. The mapping from marks to rank changes with paper difficulty and candidate numbers: NTA's own figures show the UR/EWS qualifying range moving from 720-137 (2023) to 720-162 (2024) to 686-144 (2025), so last year's rank-to-college mapping is a guide, not a promise. Fourth, remember that closing ranks describe the PAST. They tell you where the line fell last time, not where it will fall for you. Use them to build a realistic, ordered list with genuine reach, match and safe choices, and then apply the counselling rules: from Round 2 onwards, refusing an allotted seat forfeits your security deposit, so every choice you enter should be one you would actually accept.
